title: He was close enough to touch Jesus…
paragraphs: He was close enough to touch Jesus…

Because something in him knew—
being near Jesus doesn’t mean you’re surrendered to Him.
And that’s the tension we don’t talk about.

You can sit in church.
Lift your hands.
Know the songs.
Quote the verses.
And still feel that quiet, unsettling question echoing in your chest:
The disciples didn’t ask that question randomly.

Matthew writes that when Jesus said one of them would betray Him,
“they were very sorrowful and began to say to Him one after another, ‘Is it I, Lord?’” (Matthew 26:22).

Because when the light of Jesus gets close enough…
it exposes what we’ve been hiding from ourselves.

You don’t ask “Is it I?” unless somewhere deep inside…
you know you’re capable.
Capable of smiling in public while slowly drifting in private.
Some of us aren’t betraying Jesus loudly.

Through the habits we won’t surrender.
Through the convictions we keep postponing.
Through the obedience we keep negotiating.
But you still protect that one thing He’s asking you to release.
That’s where the question comes from.

But from people who have seen enough of their own heart
to stop trusting themselves more than they trust God.

AHA REVELATION:
The most dangerous place is not far from Jesus—
it’s near Him without surrender.

So the real question is not,
“Will I fail?”
“What will I do when I see what’s really inside me?”
Or bring it into the light?
Jeremiah says, “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9).
And if you don’t believe that…
why do you keep doing the very thing you prayed you’d stop?
Why do you justify what you once called sin?
Why does your private life look different from your public worship?

SPIRITUAL MIRROR STATEMENT:
You don’t struggle because you’re weak—
you struggle because you’re human without surrender.
And here’s where religion gets exposed.
Because behavior modification cannot fix a corrupted heart.
Romans 5:8 doesn’t say Christ died for improved people.
It says, “God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you cleaned up your mess.
While you were still capable of betrayal.

While you were still asking,
“Is it I?”
That’s when He chose the cross.
Jesus already knew Judas would betray Him.
Your capacity to fail did not cancel His decision to love.
But here’s the line we must not cross—
Grace is not permission to stay the same.
It is power to become new.

Some scholars interpret Judas’ story as a warning not just of betrayal,
but of proximity without transformation.

Because you can follow Jesus physically…
and still resist Him spiritually.
and still not be changed by Him.

If your version of Christianity doesn’t confront your sin,
it’s not Christianity—it’s comfort.
But when he saw his failure…
Because the difference was not perfection.
But that in Christ, failure doesn’t have to be final.
1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Because the same table that exposed sin…
also pointed to the cross that would cover it.
And the blood of Jesus doesn’t just forgive your past.
It breaks the power of what keeps pulling you back.
You are not called to live in secret cycles.
You are called to walk in freedom.
If this is hitting something deep in you…
“Jesus… it is me. And I need You.”
And watch what He does with a heart that stops hiding.
Next time, we’ll uncover why Peter ran back to Jesus… while Judas ran away.
